about: What ECMA-262 says an expression answers, written out by hand.
Every engine that claims to run a `datamodel="ecmascript"` document reads
THIS file and is measured against it. A golden captured from one of our own
engines would agree with whatever that engine currently does, including the
answers that are wrong, so each case is a claim about the LANGUAGE and the
`clause` names where a reader can check the claim against the spec rather
than against us.
Why the table is shared rather than copied: the same document answered
differently depending on which engine ran it, and no fixture in the
repository could tell — a W3C suite that is green end to end never asked
`0 && x`. A per-engine copy of the expectations reproduces exactly that
blindness, because a copy drifts toward the engine that reads it.
Readers:
sce-build/tests/ecmascript_semantics.rs  the build-time frontend, then Lua
tests/engine/EcmaScriptSemanticsTest.cpp the engine this C++ build selected
backends/kotlin/.../EcmaScriptSemanticsTest.kt  all three Kotlin engines
backends/go/lua/ecma262_semantics_test.go       go-lua and its runtime library
backends/python/tests/ecmascript/...py          lupa and its runtime library
ecmascript_semantics.rs, again                  the library as C11 embeds it,
loaded chunk by chunk
The last three read the Lua the frontend emits, from
ecma262_emitted_lua.json beside this file, because those backends never
see the ECMAScript: it was translated at build time, and what remains to
measure is their runtime library and their Lua interpreter. Go answered
four of these cases differently on the day that reader was written -- two
of its natives had no Array implementation at all -- while its W3C suite
was green, which is the same blindness described above one layer down.
The Kotlin reader measures every engine that backend offers rather than
one, because a generated Kotlin machine takes its engine as a constructor
argument: there is no build-wide choice to check, only three options handed
to a consumer. Asking all of them is what found the third defect this table
has now caught — QuickJS answered three of these cases with a ReferenceError
its Kotlin adapter invented, for variables a `<script>` block had declared.

form.condition: evaluated the way a `cond=` attribute is: the answer is ToBoolean of the value
form.value: evaluated the way an `expr=` attribute is: the value itself

expect.number: a number; an engine may hold it as an integer or a double
expect.empty: null or undefined — the two are one answer here, since ECMAScript's `==` equates them and SCXML's datamodel has no way to tell an absent property from a null one

cases.note: Lua counts only `nil` and `false` as false, so ECMAScript's wider falsy set is where a Lua-shaped rewriter answers the opposite of the language.

cases.clause: 13.13.1 the AND yields its left operand when it is falsy
13.13.1 the OR yields its right operand when the left is falsy
13.13.1 the value is an operand, not a boolean
13.13.1 the value is an operand, not a boolean
13.14 a false consequent is still the result

cases.note: `+` is addition or concatenation depending on the operands, decided at runtime.

cases.clause: 13.15.3 either side a string makes it concatenation
7.1.1 ToPrimitive of an Array joins with commas
7.2.15 array vs number: ToPrimitive gives '1,2,3', ToNumber gives NaN
7.2.15 null and undefined equal each other

cases.note: ECMAScript's `%` truncates toward zero; Lua's floors, so the two disagree on a negative left operand.

An engine that answers truthiness with `n ~= 0` calls NaN true, because NaN is not equal to anything including zero. Every backend that implements this natively has to get the comparison the other way round.

cases.clause: 13.5.3 typeof of an unresolvable reference is 'undefined'

cases.note: Lua's own `lua_isnumber` answers true for a string that parses as one, so an engine that asks it before asking about strings reports a payload that arrived as text as a number — and `typeof` is exactly how a document tells the two apart.
cases.clause: 13.5.3 typeof of a numeric string is 'string'
13.10.2 a number is not an Array

cases.note: An Array held as a 1-based Lua sequence moves every numeric index by one, and a string key must not move at all.

cases.clause: 23.1.3.1 concat appends every argument, not just the first

cases.note: Strict equality, so the coercion that `==` would perform must not happen here — a lookup that coerces finds a match a document is asking whether it has.
cases.clause: 23.1.3.14 indexOf compares with ===, so '2' does not find 2
23.1.3.1 concat spreads an Array argument and appends any other value as one element
13.3.2 member access on an object literal
13.3.3 computed member access with a non-identifier key
13.3.2 a property that is not there reads as undefined
13.3.3 a computed index is still zero-based
13.3.3 a computed string key addresses a property, unshifted
13.4.4 prefix increment yields the new value
13.4.2 postfix increment yields the old value
13.4.4 the operand is ToNumber'd, so this is not concatenation

cases.note: The `setup` of these cases is what a `<script>` body has to survive: statements, not expressions.
cases.clause: 15.2 a function expression is a value

cases.setup: function ctor() { this.bar = 0; } var o = new ctor();
cases.clause: 13.3.5 new binds `this` to a fresh object and yields it

cases.setup: var total = 0; for (var i = 0; i < 4; i++) { total += i; }
var n = 0; var i = 0; while (i < 3) { i++; if (i === 2) { continue; } n += i; }
cases.clause: 14.7.3 while, with continue skipping one iteration

cases.note: Bitwise operators run on ToInt32 of their operands and yield a number, which is not what an engine with native integers does by default.

cases.clause: 13.12 booleans are ToInt32'd, so the result is a number
12.9.4 unicode escape decodes to the character

cases.note: Reading an UNDECLARED identifier is a ReferenceError in ECMAScript, and SCE's engines raise one too, so the null case is asked of a declared variable — which is what `<data id="a"/>` produces.

§scxml-B-2 binds a `datamodel="ecmascript"` document to ECMAScript 3rd edition, and 3rd edition is a language AND a standard library. Every case in this group is a call an ordinary SCXML document makes — a bound on a counter, a substring of an event's payload, the length of a list — and none of them is an SCE extension. The groups above measure operators, which an emitter can compile; these measure the global object, which it cannot.
`length` is a property, not a method, so this also asks whether member access on a primitive string works at all.

cases.clause: 15.5.4.7 String.prototype.indexOf returns -1, not nil, when absent

cases.note: The second argument is where the search starts. An engine that drops it answers the position of the FIRST occurrence, which is the one the caller has already ruled out.
cases.clause: 15.5.4.7 String.prototype.indexOf starts at the given position

cases.note: This is the difference between parseInt and Number: a whole-string conversion refuses the trailing text, and parseInt is specified to read the prefix and stop. An engine that delegates to a strict host parser answers 0, which is a number a document cannot tell from a real one.
cases.clause: 15.1.2.2 parseInt reads the longest prefix that parses and ignores the rest

cases.note: The count, not the order: ECMAScript gives the order of a for-in enumeration and a Lua table has none to give, so the order is a normal form the shared library picks rather than a claim this table can make.
cases.clause: 15.2.3.14 Object.keys names every own enumerable property

cases.note: The AUTHOR's side of JSON, which is a different path from the one an event payload takes: `_event.data` is decoded by the host before a document ever sees it, so an engine can decode every event correctly and still have no `JSON.parse` for a `<script>` to call. No committed document reaches for it, which is why nothing noticed.
cases.clause: 15.12.2 JSON.parse yields a value whose properties are addressable
15.12.2 a JSON array parses to an Array
15.12.2 a JSON text may be a scalar, not only an object

cases.note: An Array rather than an object, so the claim survives the key order this table deliberately does not fix.

cases.clause: 15.12.2 / 15.12.3 the two are inverses over this datamodel's values
15.12.2 the result of parsing a JSON object is an object

cases.note: The constructors called as functions — the conversion an SCXML author reaches for when a payload arrives as text.
